form.reason: mechanical.gearboxes is constrained by electrical.motors but was not rewritten or justified. It still holds 148.3, 0.459 rad/s and 110 kgf·cm from the 50:1 motor rows, which conflicts with the rewritten drivetrain (86.1), balance_loop (38.7) and speed_loop (1.34). The base graph was consistent, so the revision introduced this.

Same defect as F1: the untouched gearboxes node keeps 50:1-derived values (148.3, 110 kgf·cm), contradicting the rewritten siblings (86.1, 38.7). There is no change, no justification and no owed follow-up for it, and the base did not have this inconsistency.
No node states a stall duration or what ends a stall, or compares continuous current with the maker's 25%-of-stall guidance. The base lacked this as well.
Same gap as F9: only nominal 7.2 V appears for the motor-current load, with no top-of-window or sagged voltage. This was already so in the base.

No node checks the rail at the top of the voltage window (~8.4 V fresh NiMH, general knowledge) or at the sagged bottom. The rewritten nodes carry only the nominal 7.2 V (and 6 V rated), exactly as the base nodes did.

The stale gearboxes values (148.3, 0.459, 110) contradicting the rewritten 30:1 numbers are new with the revision. The other parts of the finding were already in the base: unscaled stall current, no driver-limit comparison, no stall-duration statement, no discharge-rate check, and nominal-voltage-only checks.
The parts sheet does give the size: R1.22 and R1a.08 both read 10 × 12 × 25 mm. The finding's premise that they are null is false, so the claim has a producing source.

Stall current stays at 1.5 A @ 6 V. Scaled with R = 6/1.5 = 4 Ω to 8.4 V (general knowledge), it is about 2.1 A, and this is never derived. The base did the same for the 50:1 motor, so the gap is inherited even though the revision changed the motor.

Neither the parts sheet nor any node gives a discharge-rate limit for the #1003 cell, and nothing checks the 3.0 A draw (more at full-charge voltage) against one. The base had the same 3.0 A draw with no such check.
motor_current_draw = 1.5 A × 2 uses the 6 V rated stall current directly. No node computes V_max/R at 8.4 V, or even at 7.2 V; the base used the identical figure.

electrical.motor_drivers holds no current ratings, and nothing compares stall current to the DRV8838's 1.8 A peak or 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip (R4.06, R4.08). This matters because ~2.1 A at 8.4 V exceeds both. The base had the same omission.
power, motor_drivers and battery_pack carry only a single nominal 7.2 V, with no window top or sag under motor load. The base was identical.

No node gives the pack's charged maximum. Using general knowledge (about 8.4 V for 6 NiMH cells), the 0.833 duty cap set at 7.2 V nominal would put about 7 V on a motor whose limit is 6 V, and nothing in the graph checks this. The base had the same 6 V motor and the same nominal-only figures, so the gap was already there.

electrical.motors constrains mechanical.gearboxes, and its values changed in substance, but gearboxes was not updated, justified or listed as a follow-up. Its values are now stale against the revised drivetrain and loop nodes; in the base they were consistent.
The 1.5 A stall current is recorded only at 6 V and is never scaled to the pack's 7.2 V nominal or about 8.4 V charged voltage. The old motor's figure was handled the same way in the base.

The graph never compares motor stall current with the DRV8838's 1.8 A peak (R4.06) or 1.9 A minimum trip (R4.08). Scaled to about 8.4 V, 6 V/1.5 A gives about 2.1 A, which exceeds both. The old motor's stall current was also 1.5 A at 6 V, so the base had the same gap.

Neither the base nor the revision records any operating-to-rated ratio for the motor's voltage, current, power or temperature. The motor runs from a pack above its 6 V rating, so this missing record matters; it predates the revision.

mechanical.gearboxes still holds 148.3, 0.459 rad/s and 110 kgf·cm, computed from the 50:1 rows R1.07, R1.10 and R2.11. The revision changed the drivetrain to 86.1, the balance-loop torque to 38.7 kgf·cm and the speed-loop no-load speed to 1.34 rad/s, and gave no justification or follow-up for gearboxes. In the base these values all agreed, so the inconsistency is new.

motor_current_draw = 1.5 A × 2 uses the 6 V stall current unscaled, and motor_power_draw multiplies it by 7.2 V, mixing voltages. Nothing accounts for the higher current at 7.2–8.4 V. The base computed the same numbers from R1.03.

No node holds a continuous or peak current rating for the battery, driver or board, so the 3.0 A / 21.6 W draw is never checked against anything. The DRV8838 limits are on the parts sheet (R4.06, R4.08) but were never copied into the graph, in the base or the revision.

This is the same stale mechanical.gearboxes node as F4. electrical.motors constrains it, yet it still holds the 50:1-based ratio, speed and torque, which now contradict the drivetrain, speed-loop and balance-loop nodes the revision rewrote. It has no justification or follow-up. The base was consistent.

The finding says the size rows are null, but they are not: R1.22 and R1a.08 both read 10 × 12 × 25 mm, and both motors are listed at 9.5 g. The chassis no-change claim is therefore backed by the parts sheet.

No series element in the motor-current path (driver, connector, trace, fuse) has a declared current rating anywhere in the graph. So the path limit is never established, and the base had the same gap.

electrical.motor_drivers records only voltages and thermal resistance. No node compares stall current with the DRV8838's 1.8 A peak (R4.06) or its 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip (R4.08). The base had the same gap with the same 1.5 A motor current, so the revision only carried it forward.

No driver dissipation estimate exists. Using general knowledge, rDS(on)·I² comes to about 0.33 Ω × 1.5–1.75 A², or about 0.7–1 W, which is a 45–60 K rise at 60.9 K/W. The base never computed this either.

R1a.10 and R1a.13 are already geared output figures and R2.12 includes the 75.81:1 motor ratio, so dividing or multiplying by it double counts. The correct wheel no-load speed is about 430/2.88 rpm, roughly 15.6 rad/s. The base made the identical error with R1.10, R1.07 and R2.11, giving 0.459 rad/s and 110 kgf*cm.

Part (1) is real and introduced: supported_mass lost the battery term (330 g in the base, 165 g now). Part (2) is not a defect, because 12 × 218.5 = 2622 is written as 2620 at the packet's three-significant-figure convention.

motor_current_draw and motor_power_draw use only the 7.2 V nominal pack voltage, with no full-charge or sagged-voltage case. The base used identical formulas with R1.03, so this was already in the base.

The 1.5 A figure is rated at 6 V. The duty cap of 0.833 is computed from the nominal 7.2 V, so a full pack (about 8.4 V, general NiMH knowledge) puts about 7 V on the motor and draws about 1.75 A, which the claim that driver load is unchanged never accounts for. The base also used the unscaled 6 V figure on the 7.2 V rail.
Same defect as F2: the power, driver and motor-output nodes check only the 7.2 V nominal, with no top-of-window or sagged figure for the motor load. The base already did the same.
Duplicate of F2 and F4: the motor load is never re-checked at the top or the sagged bottom of the voltage window. That gap was already in the base.
No node records how long a stall may last or what ends it (driver trip or firmware limit). Pololu advises against long stalls of these motors (general knowledge), and the base lacked this too.

The revision dropped the battery term from drivetrain.supported_mass, giving 165 g against robot.mass of 330 g and two wheels at 165 g each; that part is introduced. The double counting of the gear ratio in no_load_speed and torque_peak (using the geared output speed and torque times the overall ratio) was already in the base, as 0.459 rad/s and 110 kgf*cm.

No comparison of stall current with the DRV8838's 1.8 A peak or 1.9 A minimum trip exists, and the base also lacked one. The finding's 2.1 A ignores the 0.833 duty cap (about 7 V and 1.75 A at 8.4 V), but that margin is thin and still unshown.
No node records an operating-to-rated stress ratio for the motor, which runs from a 7.2 to 8.4 V pack but is rated at 6 V. The base motor had the same gap.

No stress-ratio record exists for the motor or driver. The base had none either, and the load is unchanged (same 1.5 A stall). Worst-case stall current against the 1.8 A DRV8838 rating is close enough that the check matters.
The no-change reasons and supply fields cite 7.2 V only. There is no charged-top or sagged-bottom check, the same as in the base design.
Stall current is never rescaled to the operating voltage (V/R with R = 4 Ω). The base used the same unscaled 1.5 A for the old motor.

The pack load is numerically unchanged (3.0 A in both base and revision). The packet gives no maker's discharge rating for the #1003 cell, so I can't tell whether 3.0 A (about 1.4C) breaks a published limit.

No junction-temperature estimate exists. Using general datasheet reasoning: 1.5–1.8 A through 0.33 Ω at 60.9 K/W gives about 0.75–1.1 W and about 45–65 K rise, so at 85 °C ambient the margin to the 150 °C shutdown minimum is small. The base has the same gap with the same current.

Part 1 is real: R1a.10 and R1a.13 are gearmotor output figures, so using the 218.5:1 overall ratio counts the internal 75.81:1 twice. The base made the same error with 148.3. Part 2 was introduced: the drivetrain's supported mass dropped from 330 g to 165 g (without the battery), with no reason given, contradicting the robot mass and the wheel nodes.
12 × 218.5 = 2622, which is 2620 at the packet's stated three significant figures. 45.0 rad/s is the cited 430 rpm in other units, which is the same quantity and matches the base convention.

Every motor and driver check uses the 7.2 V nominal pack voltage only. At a charged 8.4 V (general NiMH knowledge), the fixed 0.833 duty cap gives the 6 V motor about 7.0 V. That gap is identical in the base, and the motor swap didn't change it.

Stall current scaled to the charged pack (4 Ω motor at 8.4 V ≈ 2.1 A uncapped, about 1.75 A with the duty cap) is never checked against the 1.8 A peak and 1.9 A trip limits. The old motor had the same 1.5 A stall figure, so the gap is in the base too.
Only a bare 60.9 K/W thermal resistance is recorded. It isn't named as RθJA and has no dissipation figure with it. The base node is identical.

The robot node's no-change reason talks only about the gear ratio. It ignores the supported-mass change (330 g to 165 g) made to the same drivetrain node in this revision, so the follow-up doesn't match the change.

The worst-case draw uses the stall current at the motor's 6 V rating without checking it at the pack's charged top, where the motor sees more than 6 V even with the duty cap. The base used the identical 1.5 A figure.

R1a.10 and R1a.13 are gearmotor-output figures that already include the 75.81:1 gearhead, so dividing or multiplying by the overall 218.5:1 double-counts it (430 rpm/2.88 ≈ 15.6 rad/s, 1.1×2.88 ≈ 3.2 kgf·cm); the base made the same error with R1.10/R1.07 and R2.11. Separately, the revision cut drivetrain supported_mass from the base's correct 330 g (whole robot with battery) to 165 g, which is a new error.

Using general knowledge that a fully charged NiMH cell is about 1.4 V (pack about 8.4 V), stall current with R = 6 V/1.5 A = 4 Ω is about 2.1 A, above the DRV8838's 1.8 A rating (R4.06). No node in the revision derives this bound, and the drivers node justifies no change using the 6 V figure alone. The base lacked the same bound with the identical 1.5 A/6 V figures, so the gap was not introduced by the revision.

Neither electrical.motors, electrical.motor_drivers nor firmware.motor_output says how long a stall may last or what ends it, and the DRV8838 trip point (1.9–3.5 A min–max, R4.08) need not catch a stall of about 1.8–2.1 A. From general knowledge, Pololu advises keeping these motors' stalls brief, so a stall limit is a real gap; the base had the same omission and the stall current is unchanged.

The revision re-sizes the gear ratio (2.88→2.47, 148.3→127.3), but no touched node states the governing limit (traction or motor), the floor μ_s or surface, or a margin. Engineering estimate (my own, not from the packet): traction likely governs by a wide margin (≈0.66 kgf·cm slip vs 94.2 kgf·cm stall). The required statement is still absent, and this sizing is what makes it owed.

The written ratio has no wheel-torque, current-margin, traction or governing-limit statement anywhere. torque_peak is a stall load case, not a margin statement, and the check uses values this revision wrote.
The gearboxes → odometry edge is unaddressed: odometry is unchanged at 1780 from R2.11. The main and speed_task notes say it was updated, and the node itself shows otherwise.
Gearboxes and speed_loop were moved to 47:19 / 127.3, but odometry keeps 1780 from 148.3 with no follow-up or justification. Two notes incorrectly say odometry carries the new constant.

mechanical.gearboxes constrains firmware.odometry, which got no update and no no_change_justified entry and still holds 1780 from R2.11. The speed_task and firmware.main notes say odometry already has the new constant, which the unchanged node shows is false.
Both nodes use the same formula, [R3.02] × ratio, for the same wheel-encoder constant. control.speed_loop now has 1530 (12 × 127.3) while firmware.odometry keeps 1780; in the base both were 1780.

firmware.odometry was left at 1780 from the old ratio even though gearboxes constrains it directly. The value now disagrees with speed_loop's 1530, and two no_change_justified notes falsely say odometry was updated.
firmware.main's note relies on a 'new counts-per-wheel-revolution constant' in firmware.odometry, but that node still holds the old 1780 derived from R2.11.
The same quantity name and formula give 1530 in control.speed_loop and 1780 in firmware.odometry. Under the new 127.3 ratio, 1780 is wrong (12 × 127.3 ≈ 1528).

The two notes treat the gearboxes → odometry follow-up as done, yet odometry was never written and that edge has no justification entry. The propagation duty is left unmet while the notes make it look met.

The speed_task and main notes skip any further follow-up because they assume odometry was already updated. The graph shows that assumption is false, so the notes avoid a follow-up that is actually owed.

The numbers are correct: odometry stays at 1780 from R2.11 = 148.3 while speed_loop has 1530 from R2.14 = 127.3. The odometry edge has no justification entry and the two notes falsely say it was updated. The base was consistent.

The revision changed gearboxes.gear_ratio from 148.3 to 127.3, but firmware.odometry, which gearboxes constrains, was neither rewritten nor given a recorded justification. Its counts_per_wheel_revolution is still 1780 ([R3.02]*[R2.11]) when it should be about 1530 ([R3.02]*[R2.14]), and that value matched the ratio in the base design.

The new justifications in firmware.speed_task and firmware.main both cite a new counts-per-wheel-revolution value in firmware.odometry. The revision never wrote that value; the node still holds the old 1780 from R2.11, so both justifications rest on a change that does not exist.

A single gearbox mount reacts its own output torque. Dividing by the robot-wide gearbox count (R2.26 = 2) has no physical basis, and the base design had reaction_moment = torque_peak with no such divisor.
81.5 − 40.8 = 40.7 kgf·cm is left unreacted, with no second reaction declared. This imbalance comes from the revision's new divisor R2.26.
The 2π/60 factor is a plain unit conversion, and 5.90 rpm is exactly 0.618 rad/s. Elsewhere the graph also cites rows in their source units and converts implicitly.

From general knowledge: the correct wheel stall torque is ≈ 0.155 N·m and the correct wheel no-load speed is 650/2.14 rpm ≈ 31.8 rad/s. The recorded 7.99 N·m and 0.618 rad/s (about 2.5 cm/s at the rim of an 80 mm wheel) come from applying the overall ratio, which the base design also did with 148.3.

It is true that no node records a traction check, a sourced mu_s or a margin, but the cited rule's text is not in the packet. So I cannot confirm that the design graph must record this check when the gear ratio changes.

650/110.2 = 5.90 rpm, which is 0.618 rad/s. Converting rpm to rad/s is only a unit conversion, and the graph routinely converts units implicitly (e.g. oz to g in the mass derivations). The recorded number does follow from the cited rows.

From general gearmotor knowledge: R1.07 is the 50:1 gearmotor's output-shaft stall torque, so wheel torque should be 0.74 × 2.14 ≈ 1.58 kgf·cm, not 0.74 × 110.2. This double-counts the internal 51.45:1 reduction, and the base made the same error with 148.3 (giving 110 kgf·cm).
firmware.motor_output limits the motor voltage to 6 V (motor_voltage_limit, max_duty_cycle = 6/7.2 = 0.833). The graph therefore records a basis for using the 6 V ratings on the 7.2 V supply.

torque_peak (81.5 kgf·cm) and no_load_speed (0.618 rad/s) apply the overall 110.2 ratio to figures that are already geared, double-counting the internal reduction. The base design had the same error with the 148.3 ratio (110 kgf·cm, 0.459 rad/s).

The new reaction_moment divisor R2.26 is unjustified and leaves the reaction unequal to torque_peak, which is a real defect the revision introduced. The 6 V/7.2 V part does not hold, because the firmware's 6 V motor limit gives the stated basis.

The base had reaction_moment = torque_peak (110 = 110); the revision's 40.8 against 81.5 is a new imbalance with no stated reason. Its side points do not change this: the unit-conversion complaint is not a defect, and the traction-check complaint cannot be checked against the rule.
The revision declares one reaction of half the applied torque, with no second reaction and no stated split, so the moments do not balance. The base design's reaction equalled its torque.

The revised reaction_moment is 0.74×110.2/R2.26(=2) = 40.8 kgf·cm. But torque_peak is already one motor's output through its own gearbox, so each gearbox mount must react about the full 81.5 kgf·cm (output minus input torque, by general gearbox statics). The base had them equal (110/110), so the revision introduced the halving.

The only distribution scheme in the revision is dividing by the number of gearboxes (R2.26). That is invalid because torque_peak is per gearbox, being one motor's stall torque times the ratio, so the mount reaction should about equal it, not half of it. The base did not have this error.

mechanical.gearboxes constrains control.balance_loop and its torque_peak changed from 110 to 71.2 kgf*cm (0.74 × 96.2), but control.balance_loop still holds 110 kgf*cm from R2.11 and has no justification keyed to mechanical.gearboxes. In the base design both values were 110, so the revision introduced the mismatch.

The stale torque_peak of 110 kgf*cm in control.balance_loop disagrees with the revised 71.2 kgf*cm in mechanical.gearboxes, and no follow-up or matching justification was written. The base design was consistent. (firmware.balance_task does also constrain control.balance_loop, but that does not cure the missing follow-up.)

control.balance_loop was not written and still carries 110 kgf*cm from the old ratio R2.11, against 71.2 kgf*cm in the revised mechanical.gearboxes, with no justification recorded for that link. The base design had both at 110.

The core defect holds: control.balance_loop got neither an update nor a justification keyed to mechanical.gearboxes. The only justification entry, on firmware.balance_task, is keyed to control.balance_loop as if that node had changed. The base design was consistent.

Using general engineering knowledge: 71.2 kgf*cm at a 40 mm wheel radius gives about 17.8 kgf of push per wheel on a 0.33 kg robot, so traction, not motor torque, always sets the limit and the lower kit ratio threatens nothing. A missing written rationale or friction coefficient is not a defect in the design itself.

Three of the four nodes that mechanical.gearboxes constrains were rewritten to match the 96.2 ratio. control.balance_loop was not and keeps torque_peak 110 kgf*cm from R2.11 with no justification keyed to mechanical.gearboxes. The base design was consistent.

The torque_peak shared by mechanical.gearboxes and control.balance_loop now disagrees (71.2 vs 110 kgf*cm), which is visible in the graph alone. The justification on firmware.balance_task is keyed as though control.balance_loop had changed. Both were 110 in the base design.
The two copies of the gearbox output torque now differ: 110 is about 55% above 71.2, and nothing reconciles them. In the base design both were 110 from R2.11.

A written value (gearboxes torque_peak 71.2 kgf*cm) is inconsistent with an unwritten one (control.balance_loop torque_peak 110 kgf*cm), so the follow-up was missed. The only related justification, on firmware.balance_task, is keyed to control.balance_loop and does not cover the gearboxes → balance loop link. The base design was consistent.

Stall torque × ratio is labelled torque_peak, the drive's maximum torque, the same way as in the base and in electrical.motors; it is not used as a continuous operating point. Using general engineering knowledge, 62.5 kgf·cm at the 40 mm wheel radius is about 15.6 kgf per wheel against roughly 0.165 kgf of normal load, so traction clearly governs and the new ratio has no torque-sizing defect.
370 − 330 g equals exactly 2 × 0.7 oz (about 39.7 g), which shows the wheel mass already inside R11.01 was added a second time. The base had both values at 330 g.

The drivetrain's supported mass changes by 40 g in the same change set where robot.mass is justified as unchanged because no part is added or removed. The numbers contradict each other, and that contradiction comes from the revision's double-count.

torque_peak and reaction_moment equal the stall torque reflected through the overall ratio, which is the correct peak (stall) torque figure and is not stated as an operating torque. The base used the same method with R2.11.

Adding R9.03 × R9.06 to a formula built on R11.01, which already includes the 80 mm wheels, double-counts about 40 g and gives 370 g against robot.mass of 330 g; the base value was a consistent 330 g. The torque half of this finding is not a defect, but the mass double-count stands.
R11.01's note says the 200 g includes the wheels, so the base 330 g already matched robot.mass and the 165 + 165 g wheel supported masses. The revision's 370 g counts the wheels a second time.

The revision raises drivetrain.supported_mass by 40 g while robot.mass stays 330 g with a 'mass unchanged' justification. The revised graph is therefore internally contradictory, which the base was not.

The 62.5 kgf·cm is presented as torque_peak, the motor's real stall-limited peak, not as an operating or design torque. Per general engineering knowledge, available wheel torque is far above the traction limit, so the missing margin statement hides no shortfall.

R11.01 (200 g) is stated to include the 80×10 mm wheels, so the added wheel-pair term double-counts about 40 g. The result is inconsistent with robot.mass and the wheel supported masses, which all remain consistent with 330 g.
The new supported_mass formula adds wheel mass that its cited row R11.01 already contains, so 370 g does not follow from the parts list; the base 330 g did.

A quantity named torque_peak equal to stall torque × gear ratio is the correct peak-torque figure and is not offered as a continuous or operating budget. The pattern is unchanged from the base apart from the new ratio.
The revision writes supported_mass = 365 g on each wheel, so the two wheels total 730 g against a robot mass of 365 g. The base had 165 g + 165 g = 330 g, which matched its total.

Each wheel's supported_mass (365 g) equals the drivetrain's total supported_mass because the revision dropped the '/ [R9.06]' division by the wheel count. The base correctly split 330 g into 165 g per wheel.

The design graph records no clearance values for any part, the packet shows no rule requiring one, and the finding itself calls it non-blocking. From general knowledge, the cage is Pololu's own accessory for this robot, and the 200 g assembled mass (R11.01) already counts it as fitted.
With the new 365 g total, each wheel should carry 365 / 2 ≈ 182.5 g. The revision wrote the full 365 g on each wheel, a factor-of-2 error that the base's divided formula did not have.

The new wheel formula '[R11.01] + [R5.07]*[R5.10]' gives the whole-robot mass, so the two wheels together declare 730 g for a 365 g robot. The base's per-wheel formula divided by R9.06 and was consistent.
The revision dropped the per-wheel division, so the wheel reactions sum to twice the robot's declared mass. The base values (165 g each, 330 g total) were consistent.
Each wheel's supported_mass equals the drivetrain and robot totals (365 g) instead of about half. This mismatch did not exist in the base.
Values written in the same revision (365 g per wheel and a 365 g total) are inconsistent: the wheels sum to 730 g. The base divided by R9.06 and was consistent.
The two wheel reactions (365 g + 365 g) do not balance the 365 g load. In the base, 165 g + 165 g balanced the 330 g total.

0.15 percent equals 0.0015 as a fraction, so the value the revision wrote contradicts the 0.15 dimensionless source it cites. The base value was 0.2 dimensionless in both nodes and was consistent.

The revision wrote 160 MHz against a source that supports 16 MHz, contradicting the unchanged electrical.mcu node. The base value was 16 MHz.

The source cited for 160 MHz supports only 16 MHz (R7.02, and electrical.mcu). The base value was 16 MHz.

From general cascade-control knowledge: the outer speed loop's bandwidth must sit below the inner tilt loop's. Sampling it at the tilt loop's 100 Hz, which already meets control.req_sample_rate, therefore gives at least the inner loop's sampling margin, and doubling from 50 Hz only improves the ratio. The rate is bounded by an argued requirement, not picked by habit.

A time unit (ms) is recorded under the quantity name sample_rate, which the rest of the graph and the base version of this node hold in Hz. That mixes up two kinds of unit (period and frequency) for one linked quantity.

No explicit ω·h ratio is written down, but tying the outer loop's rate to the inner loop's rate bounds h·ω_c for the speed loop. The speed loop's bandwidth is necessarily below the tilt loop's, and the tilt loop's 100 Hz is justified by a requirement. So the rate is not substantively defective, and raising it from 50 Hz cannot worsen aliasing or delay margins.

Separating the loops' timescales in a cascade depends on their bandwidths, not on running the outer loop at a slower sample rate. Running the outer loop at the inner loop's rate is standard practice, and on this 16 MHz ATmega32U4 it costs nothing extra because the scheduler already ticks at 100 Hz. Dropping the 'slower than' wording loses no needed justification.

The rewrite to bare R11.01 contradicts frame_and_board's formula, which explicitly subtracts R10.03, and the constituent sum of ≈164.7 g. It also leaves assembly unreconciled, with no tie to the declared gear-ratio change.

Checked against its neighbours and the parts breakdown (106 + 39.7 + 19 ≈ 165 g), the new 200 g is off by exactly the 35 g bumper-cage mass (R10.03). It is a magnitude the revision wrote that contradicts the rest of the design.
Chassis mass and assembly.unladen_mass were equal at 165 g from the same formula and now differ by 35 g (R10.03), with no stated reason for redefining the chassis mass.

The control plant model (330 g, cage subtracted) and the mechanical mass model (365 g, cage included) now disagree by 35 g, and the balance_task note falsely says plant_mass changed. Neither defect existed in the base design.

plant_mass and assembly.mass model the same physical total mass of the robot as it is now built (bumper cage fitted). They now differ by 35 g (about 9.6%) with no stated reason, while in the base design they were equal.

The note's premise that plant_mass changed is false: the balance_loop payload written in this revision keeps 330 g and the same source string. The revision wrote this false record.

plant_mass (330 g) and assembly.mass (365 g) describe the same total robot mass, and assembly constrains balance_loop. They now disagree by 35 g, whereas they matched in the base design.

assembly.mass changed by +35 g, but balance_loop.plant_mass was left identical and has no no_change_justified entry for the mechanical.assembly edge. The balance_task note falsely says the plant mass changed.

Using general motor knowledge: R = 6 V / 1.5 A = 4 Ω, so a stalled motor at 9 V draws about 2.25 A, while the design records 1.0 A per driver (power ÷ voltage only gives battery-side average current, not motor/driver current). The base used the same wrong formula (1.25 A against 1.8 A at 7.2 V); the revision kept it and made the understatement more than two-fold.

This summary combines new defects (the stale duty limit giving 7.5 V, the dropped capacity/mass with no alkaline replacement) with pre-existing ones (the power/voltage current formula and nominal-only checks, both present in the base).
pwm_duty_limit × supply_voltage = 0.833 × 9 = 7.5 V, above the 6 V motor rating (R1.02); the failing pair uses the 9 V value the revision wrote. With the base 7.2 V the product was 6 V and passed.
The checks use only nominal 9 V, with no fresh-cell top or sagged bottom, and sag cannot be computed because no internal resistance is given. The base's checks were likewise nominal-only at 7.2 V.

The base never gave the pack a discharge-current rating, and the driver figures already used the flawed formula; the revision also deleted the only capacity data and sourced nothing for alkaline cells, so the supply side has no rating to close the budget against.

Using general/datasheet knowledge: at 9 V the stall current is about 2.25 A at full duty, and about 1.875 A even with the stale 0.833 limit. That exceeds the DRV8838's 1.8 A peak rating, and full duty also exceeds the 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip (R4.06, R4.08), and the design never states this. In the base (7.2 V, 0.833 duty → 6 V, 1.5 A; 1.8 A at full duty) no exceedance existed.

The revision switched the cell from the sourced Pololu #1003 NiMH cell to an implied alkaline cell (1.5 V derived from R5.04). It names no alkaline part or datasheet and deletes the capacity and mass that came from the old part.

firmware.motor_output was re-saved with 0.833 = [R1.02]/[R5.03], still keyed to 7.2 V, with no justification, while supply_voltage became 9 V; 0.833 × 9 V = 7.5 V exceeds the 6 V motor rating. In the base, 0.833 × 7.2 V = 6 V was correct.

The current/power figures are checked only at nominal 9 V, with no fresh-cell top or sagged bottom (using general knowledge, about 9.6 V and roughly 6–6.6 V for six alkaline cells). The base had the same nominal-only check at 7.2 V.

The core defect is real: the stale R5.03-keyed duty limit against the new 9 V pack gives 7.5 V at a 6 V motor, while the correct value would be 6/9 = 0.667, and no justification was recorded. Capacity, laden mass and plant mass were also deleted without a stated reason; none of this existed in the base.
Read together, the new 9 V supply and the unchanged 0.833 duty limit put 7.5 V on a 6 V motor, and no node checks the two against each other. In the base the pair gave exactly 6 V.
All battery-based checks use only the 9 V nominal value, with no top or sagged-bottom case. The base did the same at its 7.2 V nominal, so the nominal-only practice predates the revision.

The revised electrical.battery_cell holds only a derived 1.5 V and names no cell part or chemistry, so the battery has no identified part. The base pointed to the Pololu #1003 NiMH cell, so the revision created this gap.

The revision raised supply_voltage to 9 V but left pwm_duty_limit at 0.833, still calculated from R5.03 (7.2 V). The motor now sees 9 × 0.833 ≈ 7.5 V average against its 6 V rating (R1.02). In the base, 7.2 × 0.833 = 6 V, so the problem is new.

battery_pack lists firmware.motor_output in its constrains list, and its supply_voltage changed. The motor_output node was re-saved with the same value and the same R5.03 source, with no recomputation and no no_change_justified entry. The edge was never reconciled.

Switching to alkaline dropped the only cell part reference (#1003) and deleted charge_capacity and mass_per_cell with nothing to replace them. The pack mass and the assembly/plant masses that depended on it also disappeared, so the battery's ratings are no longer documented.

Working it out from the written values: 9 V (written by the revision) × 0.833 ≈ 7.5 V, which exceeds the 6 V motor rating (R1.02). The driver side was updated to R5.04 but the firmware duty limit was not.

The parts sheet has no alkaline discharge-rate or discharge-curve data, so the packet cannot show whether the 2.0 A pack draw is within or beyond an alkaline cell's limit. The lack of a named part is already covered by F1/F4.

current_draw = 6 V × 1.5 A / V_pack is power-balanced supply current, not motor stall current at pack voltage. Using Ohm's-law scaling (my general engineering knowledge), stall current is 1.5 × 9/6 = 2.25 A, or 1.875 A at the stale 0.833 duty, both above the DRV8838's 1.8 A. The revision's 1.0 A hides this. The base used the same under-scaled method (1.25 A) and the revision recomputed with it.

The re-derived currents use only the nominal 9 V. From typical alkaline datasheets (general knowledge), six fresh cells sit around 9.6 V, which makes the over-voltage and over-current at the stale duty limit worse. The base also used only the nominal 7.2 V with no voltage window, and the revision repeated that when it recomputed the values.

The revision leaves electrical.imu.current_draw at the normal-mode 0.9 mA (R8.05), yet rewrites control_board.sensor_power_draw to 3.3 V × 1.25 mA = 4.13 mW (R8.04) for the same IMU in high-performance mode. The balance_loop claim that the IMU current changed is contradicted by the unchanged node. In the base, 0.9 mA and 2.97 mW agreed.
With the rule numbers redacted, the finding names no quantity, node or condition, so there is nothing in the packet to check it against.

balance_loop's new no_change_justified says the IMU supply current changed, but the rewritten electrical.imu node holds exactly the base values (0.9 mA, 3.3 V). The graph contradicts itself, and this is new to the revision.

At 416 Hz the LSM6DS33 runs in high-performance mode (general datasheet knowledge, matching the revision's own note), so 1.25 mA applies. The IMU node keeps 0.9 mA while control_board now uses 1.25 mA (4.13 mW); in the base both agreed at 0.9 mA / 2.97 mW.

electrical.imu was rewritten as the follow-up to the sample-rate change but keeps the stale normal-mode 0.9 mA. That conflicts with the high-performance mode now required and with control_board's R8.04-based derivation, so the follow-up exists only in form.

Correct: the IMU node still says 0.9 mA (R8.05, normal mode) while control_board's sensor power assumes 1.25 mA (R8.04, high-performance mode) for the same chip in the same mode, and balance_loop's justification wrongly says the node's current changed.
The rewritten electrical.imu node keeps the normal-mode 0.9 mA, while control_board's re-derived figure assumes 1.25 mA. The base was consistent (0.9 mA / 2.97 mW), so the revision introduced this.

The revision's own values disagree: the 416 Hz high-performance-mode rationale and control_board's 4.13 mW both imply 1.25 mA, but the IMU node records 0.9 mA, and balance_loop's 'current changed' text does not match that node.

The constrained IMU node was not actually updated after the sample-rate and mode change: its current, voltage and sources are identical to the base. The upstream justification claiming the current changed does not hold, so the follow-up was missed.

The revision wrote electrical.imu.current_draw as 1.25 mW, but R8.04 is 1.25 mA, a current. Its own control_board derivation (3.3 V × 1.25 mA = 4.13 mW) treats that same figure as a current, while the base record (0.9 mA) had the right unit.
Labelling the R8.04 current figure in mW is a unit-kind error. It contradicts the same revision's sensor_power_draw derivation from R8.04 and replaces a base record that correctly used mA.
R8.04 is a supply current in mA, and the revision's own [R8.03]*[R8.04] power derivation confirms it. Recording current_draw in mW is wrong, and the base record (mA) did not have this error.
The value 1.25 is R8.04's mA current copied over unconverted under a power unit. That is a unit mismatch in a quantity the revision itself wrote; the base record used mA correctly.

The unit changed from mA to mW without the number being converted (and the two units can't be converted anyway). That clashes with both R8.04 and the revision's own power derivation; the base design had a correct mA record.
The base held 0.9 mA and the revision wrote 1.25 mW, which conflicts with R8.04's mA unit and with every other current_draw in the graph (mA or A). The defect is newly introduced.

The core defect is real: a current recorded in mW, which also conflicts with the revision's 4.13 mW sensor_power_draw, while the base used mA. The extra claim about which standards category applies cannot be checked from the packet, but it doesn't change the verdict.

The revision put a 2.5 ms period into firmware.balance_task's field named sample_rate, while control.balance_loop and firmware.imu_driver keep sample_rate in Hz, so the field now holds a period rather than a frequency. The base had 100 Hz there, consistent with the rest of the graph.

The base's 100 Hz was likewise justified only as meeting the minimum, with no bandwidth ratio, so the missing justification was already there.

Both parts hold. The balance_loop node has no note saying no change is needed.

The new source text plainly states no ratio of 400 Hz to any bandwidth, only a general benefit and minimum-rate compliance, so this can be decided from the packet. The base 100 Hz source ('meeting the required minimum loop rate') has the same gap.

electrical.imu constrains control.balance_loop, and the revised balance_loop node neither reflects the IMU current change nor carries a no_change_justified entry for that link. The revision did write such an entry elsewhere (regulator_5v for control_board), so this one is missing.

firmware.balance_task.sample_rate is now 2.5 ms, a period, while the sibling sample_rate fields are 400 Hz and 833 Hz; all three were in Hz in the base. The values agree (2.5 ms = 400 Hz) but the quantity kind does not.
Same defect as F6: the revision wrote a period under a field name used everywhere else for a rate in Hz, which the base design did not do.
The rewritten imu_driver source cites a 150 Hz balance-task rate, but firmware.balance_task records 100 Hz. The base imu_driver source gave no number, so this contradiction is new.

No node in either graph gives a crossover or bandwidth figure, and nothing in the packet requires stating a ratio to one. Raising the rate from 100 Hz to 150 Hz can only improve the sampling-to-bandwidth margin; this used general control knowledge. Lacking a stated ratio is not a defect the revision introduced.

balance_loop went to 150 Hz and constrains balance_task. The task was rewritten but kept 100 Hz, even though its source says it equals the loop period, and no no_change_justified entry was added. In the base, both were 100 Hz.

Both claims hold. The task's 100 Hz conflicts with the 150 Hz loop it says it matches, and the IMU source's '150 Hz balance-task rate' conflicts with the task's recorded 100 Hz. Neither conflict exists in the base.

The task (100 Hz, 'equal to the balance-loop period') is inconsistent with the 150 Hz loop that constrains it, with no justification recorded, and no node records a 150 Hz task rate. The base was consistent at 100 Hz.
The IMU driver source asserts a 150 Hz balance-task rate that contradicts the task node's recorded 100 Hz. This is new in the revision.

The revision implies a 150 Hz task rate in the IMU node but records 100 Hz in the task node, while the loop the task is said to match is at 150 Hz. It is an internal contradiction the revision created.
The '150 Hz balance-task rate' in the IMU source is contradicted by balance_task.sample_rate = 100 Hz. The base had no such conflict.
The firmware task runs at 100 Hz while the control loop, argued at about 6.7 ms, is 150 Hz, so the rate that runs is not the rate that was argued. In the base, both were 100 Hz.

The main claim holds: the 150 Hz loop change did not reach balance_task and no justification was given. The secondary point about the IMU-current edge to balance_loop is weak, since balance_loop was itself rewritten and none of its quantities depend on IMU current, but the main defect is real.

torque_peak went from the two-motor value 2 × 0.74 kg·cm ≈ 0.145 N·m to one motor's datasheet stall torque, with no derivation. It now disagrees with chassis.reaction_moment (still 0.145 N·m) and with the revision's own claim that the torque limits are unchanged. Unit conversion from general engineering knowledge.
The new value is the single-motor stall torque copied in place of the two-motor figure [R1.07] × [R1.25], with no arithmetic shown, which understates the actuator torque by half.
The changed torque_peak was neither passed on to firmware.balance_task nor excused there. The only justification is keyed to angle_controller and wrongly says torque is unaffected.
The justification text conflicts with the torque_peak value changed in the same write. The unwarranted halving to a single-motor value is the defect behind the conflict.

balance_loop constrains firmware.balance_task. The revision changed a quantity on balance_loop but gave firmware.balance_task no follow-up and no justification; the only justification on record is keyed to angle_controller. The underlying fix is to restore the correct torque value.
The justification says actuator torque limits are unchanged, yet the same write halves torque_peak on that node, so the record contradicts itself. A gain change gives no reason for any torque change.

The derived combined-torque value (0.145 N·m, matching the chassis reaction moment) was replaced by a single-motor literal. The robot has two motors (R1.25) and the plant mass is the whole robot, and no analysis supports the change.

The justification denies any torque-limit change, but the same write halves torque_peak, and the change is neither propagated nor justified toward firmware.balance_task. Both parts of the finding hold.

0.0726 N·m with the 3073 specs URL is the per-motor stall_torque from electrical.motor_left/right, copied as is. The balance loop drives both motors, so the right value is double that, as the base derivation shows.
The stated claim that actuator torque limits are unchanged conflicts with the same write changing torque_peak from 0.145 to 0.0726 N·m. That torque change is itself unwarranted.
Same contradiction as F3/F7: the revision's own torque_peak edit contradicts its justification text, and nothing in a gain increase calls for halving the torque.

The torque_peak change on balance_loop has no follow-up or justification on firmware.balance_task, which balance_loop constrains. The existing justification covers only the gain coming into balance_loop.

The base torque_peak was [R1.07]*[R1.25] = 0.74 kg·cm × 2 = 0.145 N·m (unit conversion from general knowledge); the revision replaces it with one motor's 0.0726 N·m stall torque, which drops the two-motor factor without any computation or justification, so the balance loop's peak torque is understated by half.

After the revision, torque_peak (0.0726 N·m) disagrees with mechanical.chassis.reaction_moment (0.145 N·m, same derivation), and the revision's own no_change_justified says the actuator torque limits are unchanged while the same write halves torque_peak.

The same write both claims the actuator torque limits are unchanged and halves torque_peak without support, so the revision contradicts itself. The propagation half is weak, though: firmware.balance_task holds no torque quantity, so a missing follow-up to it has little substantive effect.

The revision raises the outer wheel-speed gain 16x, from 0.5 to 8, giving only a stated purpose: no derivation, no margin check, and a no_change_justified note that never addresses loop stability. Using general cascade-control knowledge (not the packet), the outer loop should be much slower than the inner one; 0.5 against the inner tilt gain of 20 kept that separation, but 8 against 20 likely does not on this unstable plant (and 8 demands full-scale tilt at one-eighth full wheel speed, so it may also saturate), so the defect is new to the revision.

R1.18 (0.16 kgf·cm) × R1.25 (2) = 0.32 kgf·cm ≈ 0.0314 N·m (I used the general-knowledge factor 0.0980665), so the recorded 0.32 N·m does not match its source. torque_limit is new in this revision, so the error was introduced.

The correct value is 0.16×2×0.0980665 = 0.0314 N·m, not 0.32. The sibling torque_peak (0.74×2×0.0980665 = 0.145) shows the design converts units correctly elsewhere. The quantity was newly written by the revision.
The stated source gives 0.0314 N·m once kgf·cm is converted, and torque_peak checks out with the same factor, so the recorded 0.32 N·m is unsupported. The quantity is new in the revision.
The value is the raw kgf·cm product with the conversion to N·m left out; correctly converted it is about 0.0314 N·m. The revision introduced this quantity.

The conversion is missing, so the value is about 10.2× too high. As written, the 'limit' of 0.32 N·m also exceeds the 0.145 N·m stall-torque-based torque_peak, which is physically inconsistent. Both problems come from the new torque_limit.
The arithmetic is confirmed: 0.32 kgf·cm ≈ 0.0314 N·m. torque_peak is unchanged from the base and correctly converted, and the new limit is wrongly larger than the stall-derived peak.
The cited rows give 0.32 kgf·cm ≈ 0.0314 N·m, not 0.32 N·m, while torque_peak's conversion matches its recorded value. The defect is in the newly added quantity.

The raw kgf·cm number was relabelled N·m; the correct value is about 0.0314 N·m. As written, 0.32 N·m is more than twice the combined stall torque_peak of 0.145 N·m, which a saturation limit cannot be. The revision introduced it.

Confirmed: torque_limit should be about 0.0314 N·m. torque_peak (0.145 N·m) and plant_mass (0.97 oz × 6 ≈ 165 g, giving 330 g) show the design converts units elsewhere. The new torque_limit breaks that practice.
No row on the cited 3073 specs page converts to 513 rad/s (R1.10 gives 68.1 and R1.17 gives 51.3 rad/s). 513 = 490·π/3, a tenfold conversion error in a quantity the revision added.
No correct conversion of R1.10 or R1.17 gives 513 rad/s, and the value matches a tenfold error on 51.3 rad/s. The source does not support the new quantity.
The same specs URL already gives 68.1 rad/s in the node, and no row for this motor converts to 513 rad/s. The new speed_limit is contradicted by its own cited source.

The cited page's rows do not support 513 rad/s, and the node's own no_load_speed of 68.1 rad/s for the same shaft shows a 513 rad/s limit can never be reached. The base node had no speed_limit, so the revision introduced this.
The recorded source does not give the value: no parts-sheet row for the 3073 converts to 513 rad/s, and the same URL backs 68.1 rad/s in the same node.
The arithmetic is right: 490 rpm is 51.3 rad/s, 650 rpm is 68.1 rad/s, and 68.1/2.88 is 23.6 rad/s at the wheel. The new 513 rad/s limit is unsupported and far above what the drive can reach.

513 = 490·π/3 is confirmed, a factor-of-ten error against the correct π/30. The value is about 7.5× the no-load speed recorded in the same node, so the new quantity is unsupported and self-inconsistent.
The rate limit the revision declared rests on a source that does not support 513 rad/s (the same URL gives 68.1 rad/s via R1.10), so the declaration is not properly sourced.
513 rad/s matches no conversion of the 3073 rows and is about 7.5× the node's own no-load speed. It therefore cannot work as the set-point clamp that firmware.balance_task's justification says it is.
The bare-URL source implies a direct copy with only a unit conversion, but no row converts correctly to 513 rad/s (R1.10 converts to 68.1). The value the revision wrote is unsupported by its source.
The parts-sheet record of the cited page (R1.10 giving 68.1 rad/s, and also R1.17 giving 51.3 rad/s) contradicts the 513 rad/s attributed to it. The revision added this quantity.

The same part, source and value are recorded in J on one motor and W on the other. Power in joules is a unit error, and this revision introduced it.
The cited Pololu spec (row R1.20) gives 0.80 W, not J. The recorded claim therefore does not match its own source, and the field is new in this revision.

No stall-current bound is computed at the pack's top voltage. The base driver sizing (output_current 1.5 A) already had the same omission.

The base drivers were already sized against 1.5 A, so that part is inherited and the revision restates it.

The new justification checks the driver only against the 1.5 A stall current at the motor's rated 6 V. Scaling to the pack voltage (7.2 V nominal, about 8.4 V when fresh, from general NiMH knowledge) gives 1.8–2.1 A, at or above the DRV8838's 1.8 A rating. No top-of-window or sagged-voltage check exists in the revision, but the base also checked only the single nominal 7.2 V, so the gap is pre-existing and carried into the new value.

The base cell was sourced to the Pololu #1003 product page. The revised cell's 1.5 V is only parts-sheet arithmetic (R5.04/R5.10), with no part or datasheet for the new cell, and capacity and mass were deleted.

current_draw = 6 V × 1.5 A / V_pack makes stall-derived current fall as voltage rises, giving 1.0 A instead of about 2.25 A. The base used the same backward formula (1.25 A instead of about 1.8 A at 7.2 V), and the revision only re-applied it.

Using the general DC-motor rule I_stall ≈ V/R with R = 4 Ω, true stall at 9 V is 2.25 A, but the revision records 1.0 A from a power-over-voltage formula that scales the wrong way. The base used the same formula and gave 1.25 A at 7.2 V against a true 1.8 A, so the defect was already there.

Having no separate average-versus-continuous and peak-versus-limit closure is a structural gap carried over from the base. The resulting unshown exceedance (2.25 A against 1.8 A) arises only at the new 9 V pack.
Only the 9 V nominal is used, with no check at fresh-cell open-circuit voltage or at sagged voltage. The base likewise used only 7.2 V nominal.

The 1.0 A figure understates the 2.25 A true stall current and is even below the 1.5 A rated-voltage stall current. The base value of 1.25 A at 7.2 V had the same inverted scaling, so a different number does not make this a new defect.
The revision uses only the 9 V nominal pack voltage, with no check at the top or sagged bottom of the voltage range. The base did the same with 7.2 V nominal, so the defect is already in the base.

At 9 V the true 2.25 A stall current exceeds the 1.8 A peak rating and the 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip, yet no comparison or behaviour declaration to control or firmware is made. At the base's 7.2 V the true stall current was 1.8 A, within both limits, so the exceedance is new.

The cell changed from the sourced NiMH #1003 to an unnamed alkaline cell. Its 1.5 V is just the 9 V pack voltage divided by six, with no part number or cell datasheet, and the base cell was fully sourced.

The 2.25 A stall exceeding the 1.8 A limit, the unnamed new cell chemistry and the deleted capacity ratings are introduced by the revision. The missing true worst-case budget entry was already in the base.
1.0 A at 9 V below 1.5 A at 6 V is the same inverted scaling the base had (1.25 A at 7.2 V), because the revision reused the base formula.

Both the pack figure (2.0 A) and the driver figure (1.0 A) are rated-voltage power divided by pack voltage, so the true worst case (2 × 2.25 = 4.5 A) is missing. The base had the same omission with 2.5 A and 1.25 A against a true 3.6 A and 1.8 A.

The check against the 1.8 A limit passes only because it uses the understated current. The true 2.25 A exceeds both the 1.8 A limit and the 1.9 A minimum trip, a condition that did not exist at 7.2 V, where true stall was 1.8 A.

No node states or sources an IMU filter bandwidth, so the design cannot show it sits below half the 100 Hz rate the balance task uses the samples at. From general LSM6DS33 datasheet knowledge, the default ODR-linked accelerometer filter (about 100 Hz at 208 Hz, about 200 Hz at 416 Hz) is above 50 Hz in both cases. The base design at 208 Hz had exactly this gap, so the revision carried it forward rather than creating it.

The failing sub-check (a) is the same missing filter bandwidth: no node in either design states or sources one, and from datasheet knowledge the default bandwidth at either ODR is above half the 100 Hz rate the samples are used at. The base design at 208 Hz already lacked it, so the defect was not introduced by the revision.

The revision raised electrical.imu current_draw from 0.9 to 1.25 mA, and electrical.imu constrains control.balance_loop. The revised control.balance_loop changes only sample_rate and has no no_change_justified entry for electrical.imu, although the revision used that convention on regulator_5v; the base had no such change, so the gap is new.

Same defect as F1: the changed IMU current never reaches control.balance_loop, which it constrains, and no reason is recorded. The balance_loop rewrite only follows firmware.balance_task's 200 Hz rate; the gap is absent from the base, where current_draw was unchanged.

The revision changed firmware.balance_task.sample_rate (100→400 Hz) and electrical.imu.current_draw (0.9→1.25 mA), and both nodes list control.balance_loop in constrains. But the revised control.balance_loop has no no_change_justified entry for either edge, and its 400 Hz write came first (the task's source says it copies the loop period), so neither edge is closed. The revision used no_change_justified properly on electrical.regulator_5v, so the convention applies, and the base had none of these changes, so the gap is new.

The 400 Hz source gives only a delay-reduction reason and a comparison to the 100 Hz minimum. No node gives a crossover or closed-loop bandwidth, so the ratio the antipattern asks for is missing. From general knowledge, the tilt dynamics are only a few Hz, so 400 Hz is probably ample in practice. The base 100 Hz entry ('meeting the required minimum loop rate') had the same missing justification.

Same defect as F1. The changed quantities on firmware.balance_task and electrical.imu each have an edge to control.balance_loop. That node has no later change and no no_change_justified entry naming either source, unlike the justified control_board→regulator_5v edge in the same revision. This was introduced by the revision, since the base changed neither quantity.

The revision raises the loop rate from 100 to 150 Hz 'for tighter tilt regulation', a qualitative goal. The graph has no crossover or natural frequency, so 150 Hz is never tied to a stated ratio, yet the rise forces the IMU into high-performance mode and raises its current. The base's 100 Hz was simply a stated requirement; the unsupported reason for changing the rate comes with this revision.

control.balance_loop is itself rewritten in this revision, and none of its quantities (gear ratio, no-load speed, plant mass, sample rate, torque) depend on the IMU's supply current. The 0.9 to 1.25 mA change has nothing it needs to change in that node; the only gap is that no entry names the IMU edge.

The propagation part fails for the same reason as F2: balance_loop is rewritten and has no quantity that depends on IMU current. The second part is correct: the new 150 Hz rate is justified only by prose ('tighter tilt regulation'), with no ratio to any closed-loop bandwidth in the graph, and that gap comes with this revision.

The base design's firmware.motor_output.pwm_duty_limit of 0.833 (6/7.2) holds the average motor voltage at 6 V, so stall current is about 1.5 A at nominal pack voltage and about 1.75 A at 8.4 V fresh (general PWM-averaging knowledge, R = 4 Ω). Both are below the 1.8 A limit, so the driver-sizing claim holds; the reviewer's 1.8–2.1 A figures ignore the duty limit.

Rated-voltage stall current is not being used at a higher motor voltage: the firmware duty cap of 0.833 holds the average motor voltage to 6 V at 7.2 V nominal, giving 1.5 A. At 8.4 V fresh this is about 1.75 A, still below the 1.8 A current_limit and the 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip (R4.08). The reviewer's 1.8 A and 2.1 A apply only at 100% duty, which the design does not allow.

The antipattern does not apply because the motor never sees the full pack voltage: the base design's pwm_duty_limit = R1.02/R5.03 fixes the effective motor voltage at 6 V nominal. The worst case at a fresh pack is about 1.75 A, below the driver's recorded 1.8 A limit (general PWM-averaging knowledge used).

With the duty limit, the peak stall current is 1.5 A nominal and about 1.75 A fresh, so the comparison against the 1.8 A limit passes. The finding is also wrong that R4.06 and R4.08 are null: the sheet gives 0–1.8 A peak output current and a 1.9 A minimum overcurrent trip, which the scaled currents stay below.

The revision halves the requirement floor from 100 Hz to 50 Hz for a convenience reason, with no analysis, and no issued specification exists to allow it. The base held 100 Hz, so the widening is new.

The minimum sample rate for an open-loop-unstable balancer is a safety-relevant floor. The revision lowers it using only a prose reason and no quantitative analysis anywhere in the graph; the balance_loop note follows the change correctly but does not justify it.

The 50 Hz value is newly written, so the exemption for conditions already in the design does not apply. It states no ratio to the closed-loop bandwidth and rests on a convenience reason, so it is an unexcused widening.
With no issued specification there is no allowance. 'Admit slower test builds' is not a sourced control analysis, so neither excuse covers the halved threshold.

Nothing in the graph shows a 50 Hz loop is stable for this unstable plant; by general control knowledge, 50 Hz is only about 5–10 times a likely balance bandwidth. The floor was nonetheless lowered from the base's 100 Hz.

The new 50 Hz value is a round number picked for convenience with no stated ratio to the closed-loop bandwidth, which is the antipattern the finding cites. The value and its convenience reason are both new in this revision.
The requirement node's only job is to constrain the balance loop. It was lowered to 50 Hz without any sourced stability analysis, which weakens the acceptance criterion with nothing to support it.
No issued specification and no sourced analysis support the 100-to-50 Hz widening, so it is an unexcused weakening of a safety-relevant threshold, introduced by this revision.
Halving the sample-rate floor with only a convenience reason, and with no allowance or analysis behind it, is an unexcused widening that appears for the first time in this revision.

The revision did write follow-up changes to electrical.driver_left and electrical.driver_right: both rewritten nodes add continuous_current_draw (0.35 A = [R1.01]*[R1.19]/[R5.03]) and continuous_output_current (0.42 A), neither of which is in the base nodes. So no no_change_justified entry was needed, and the per-driver 0.35 A is consistent with the pack's 0.7 A for two drivers.

The pack's new continuous quantities (0.7 A, 5.04 W, both arithmetically correct) are carried into both driver nodes, which the revision rewrote with a matching per-driver continuous_current_draw of 0.35 A. The claim that two of the four constrained nodes got no follow-up is contradicted by the revision's own written nodes.

The parts sheet (R8.09/R8.10, copied verbatim from LSM6DS33 DocID027423 Rev 4 Table 3) lists 13 Hz as the lowest gyro and accelerometer ODR, and R8.06 gives IddLP at ODR = 13 Hz, so 13 Hz matches the cited source. From general datasheet knowledge, '12.5 Hz' is ST's register-table name for the same setting, not a different rate.

The ODR table in this packet's source (R8.09: 13, 26, 52, 104, 208 … 6664 Hz) does contain 13 Hz as its lowest entry. The value is therefore supported by its source, and the finding's claimed table does not match the datasheet the design cites.

The 13 Hz magnitude matches the parts sheet's lowest LSM6DS33 ODR (R8.09/R8.10) and the low-power current condition (R8.06), so there is no unsupported deviation. 13 is the source's exact stated value, consistent with the sibling node's 208 Hz from the same table.

The cited datasheet as recorded on the parts sheet lists 13 Hz, not 12.5 Hz, as the lowest ODR. The written value equals the source value, and a value copied verbatim as 13 does not break the three-significant-figure convention.

490 rpm × 2π/60 = 51.3 rad/s, so the new `speed_limit` and `input_speed_limit` values are the 'speed at max efficiency' row (R1.17), cited straight to the spec page as though the maker states a speed limit; the spec page states no such limit, and an efficiency operating point is not a clamp or gearbox input rating. A clamp at that speed would need its own 'design:' rationale. None of these quantities exist in the base design, so the revision introduced the mislabel (I used general motor-datasheet knowledge to judge this).

Using general mechanics knowledge: the gearboxes are mounted to the chassis, so the reaction at stall is the wheel-axle torque, 0.0726 N·m × 2.88 ≈ 0.209 N·m per side (about 0.418 N·m total). The new chassis justification (2 × 0.0726 = 0.145 N·m) therefore leaves out the external stage. The 0.145 N·m chassis reaction_moment and the identically sourced torque_peak were already in the base design, while the justification text is new; the encoder justification correctly holds.

The new motor_reaction_moment of 0.0726 N·m is the gearmotor's stall torque, not multiplied by the node's own external gear_ratio of 2.88, so the reaction at the axle is understated (should be ≈0.209 N·m per side). It is then used to keep the chassis reaction_moment at 0.145 N·m, a value that was already too low in the base design.

The new gearbox quantity copies the motor's own stall torque (0.0726 N·m) into a node that also holds gear_ratio 2.88 and overall_gear_ratio 148.3. The stall bound at the wheel axle is about 2.88 times higher (≈0.209 N·m), so the value disagrees with its own node; this quantity did not exist in the base design.

supply_voltage_margin is R7.09 (the 6.0 V abs. max) minus the 5 V supply, so it uses a stress rating as the operating limit; the base node had no such quantity. F1 wrongly says R7.05 is null (it gives 2.7–5.5 V), but the defect it describes is real.
The new margin uses the abs. max row R7.09 as the operating limit, which conflicts with the rule that absolute maximum ratings are stress ratings only; this is not in the base.
The new margin compares the abs. max 6.0 V against the 5 V operating supply, which is exactly the antipattern; the revision introduced it.
The written margin value is derived from the abs. max rating and treats it as an operating limit, so it is inconsistent with the standards; the base node had no margin quantity.
max_supply_voltage is copied from the abs. max row R7.09 and used as the limit in the new margin, which is designing to the absolute maximum rating; neither quantity is in the base.
The 1.0 V margin is computed from R7.09 (abs. max) and not from the recommended operating range R7.05 (2.7–5.5 V, which would give 0.5 V); the revision added it.
The new margin is R7.09 − R7.03 = 1.0 V, which compares an absolute-maximum stress rating directly with the 5 V operating supply; the base had no such quantities.
The margin comes from the abs. max figure rather than an operating-condition rating, so it is not backed by a proper operating limit. This is the same defect the revision introduced.

Graph quantities hold only value/unit/source, and no base node records conditions. An absolute-maximum rating (per general datasheet knowledge) applies under all conditions, so a missing condition here is not a design defect; the real problem is using it as a limit at all.
Both new quantities use an Absolute Maximum Ratings value as an operating limit, which is inconsistent with the standards; the revision introduced this.
Same as F6: the schema carries no condition field, the base never records conditions, and an abs. max rating is not given at a test condition, so the missing condition is not itself a defect.
supply_voltage_margin = 6.0 V (abs. max) − 5 V uses a stress rating as the comparison limit (general datasheet knowledge: abs. max is not an operating limit); the revision added it.

The new supply_voltage_margin is computed as R7.09 − R7.03 = 6.0 − 5 V. R7.09 is labelled as the absolute-maximum figure (Atmel datasheet §29.1; from general datasheet knowledge, that section is the Absolute Maximum Ratings list, not an operating limit). The margin should be taken against the recommended operating maximum of 5.5 V (R7.05), which gives 0.5 V, and no derating basis is stated, so the recorded 1.0 V margin is overstated. The base MCU node had no margin quantity at all, so the revision introduced this defect. The finding calls the margin a 'ratio' although it is a difference in volts, and I could not check the standards file it cites, but the defect it describes is real.

The new no_load_current_draw (6 V × 150 mA / 7.2 V = 0.125 A) and the stall budget it is compared against scale the same way with pack voltage, so the voltage cancels and no-load is 10% of stall at the charged top (~8.4 V, general NiMH knowledge) and at the sagged bottom alike. A check at the ends of the window would give the same answer, so the nominal-only figure hides no defect; the stall budget itself is unchanged from the base.

The no_change_justified comparison doesn't depend on voltage: no-load and stall figures are both motor current × 6 V / V_pack, so their ratio stays 0.1 anywhere in the window. Even at the +50% no-load tolerance (general datasheet knowledge) it stays well below stall, so the conclusion that nothing needs to propagate holds without separate top or bottom checks.

Same issue as F1/F2: the revision-written no-load figure is correct and the comparison relying on it holds at every pack voltage, because both quantities scale identically with 1/V_pack. Leaving out window-end figures therefore leaves no hidden defect in the design.

The revision does write mechanical.gearboxes: gear_ratio goes from 148.3 to 86.1 (R2.10), no_load_speed from 0.459 to 1.34 rad/s (1100 rpm / 86.1; the rpm-to-rad/s conversion is general knowledge), and torque_peak/reaction_moment from 110 to 38.7 kgf*cm (0.45 * 86.1). Because the downstream node was changed, the propagation rule is met and the finding's premise is false.

The revision changes the ratio (2.88 to 2.47, overall 148.3 to 127.3, torque_peak 110 to 94.2 kgf·cm), yet no node it wrote states which limit governs, gives a traction check (there is no friction coefficient or surface anywhere in the graph or parts sheet), or states a margin. My general-knowledge check (94.2 kgf·cm / 4 cm ≈ 23.6 kgf at the tyre against ~0.165 kg per wheel, needing μ ≈ 140) shows traction governs by a wide margin, so this is a missing check and margin statement, and it was triggered by the revision's re-sizing of the ratio.

The revision wrote reaction_moment as 'derived: [R1.07] * [R2.17]' = 0.74 × 110.2 ≈ 81.5 kgf*cm, with no division by R2.26 and no 40.8 value. The finding describes a source and number that aren't in the revised node, and the stall torque × overall ratio value that is there correctly gives one gearbox's reaction moment (general engineering judgement).

The revision does rewrite control.balance_loop: its torque_peak goes from 110 to 71.2 kgf*cm, with source changed to [R1.07] * [R2.20]. That matches the new gearboxes value (0.74 × 96.2 = 71.2), so the node was followed up directly by recomputation. The no_change_justified entry on firmware.balance_task covers that node's own edge and is not the only follow-up.

The formula [R11.01] − [R10.03] + [R5.07]·[R5.10] works out to 200 g − 35 g + 6 × 0.97 oz (about 165 g) = 330 g. It takes the assembled mass, which already includes the wheels, removes the bumper cage and adds the batteries; no wheel-mass row (R9.03) is added again, so nothing is counted twice. This node is also the same as in the base design.

The revised electrical.imu node records current_draw as 0.9 mA, not 90 mA. That matches R8.05 (gyro + accel normal mode, 0.9 mA at 208 Hz) from the cited LSM6DS33 datasheet and fits the 0.35 mA reduction from 1.25 mA stated in the justification, so there is no decimal error and the source supports the value.

The revision did write control.tilt_estimator, setting sample_rate to 200 Hz with the source 'fusion at every IMU read, twice the balance loop rate'. That matches firmware.imu_driver's 200 Hz one-sample-per-update relationship and still meets the 100 Hz minimum in control.req_sample_rate, so the claimed mismatch and the missing follow-up do not exist. From general datasheet knowledge, the LSM6DS33 also offers a 208 Hz output data rate (R8.09/R8.10), which supports 200 Hz reads.

The revised control.speed_loop node gives no_load_speed as 0.459 rad/s, not 4.38, which is 650 rpm / 148.3 = 4.38 rpm converted correctly (×2π/60). The value is unchanged from the base and matches mechanical.gearboxes, so the unconverted value the finding describes is not in the revision.

The revision actually wrote 32.2 K/W, not 3.22 K/W. That value matches the DRV8838 datasheet's RθJB in parts-sheet row R4.16, so it has a source that gives it and the unsourced-value defect described does not exist. Whether swapping junction-to-ambient (60.9) for junction-to-board (32.2) is the right figure is a separate question that this finding does not raise.

The revision set control.req_sample_rate to 50 Hz, not 5 Hz as the finding says, and the balance loop, tilt estimator and IMU driver all still run at 100 Hz, so the requirement is met. A 'design:' source with no crossover-ratio computation is the same provenance style the base used for its 100 Hz value, and the packet treats that as a valid way to source a design choice, so the defect described does not exist.

The revised node gives torque_peak as 219 in kgf*cm, not N*m, and 0.74 kgf*cm × 148.3 × 2 = 219.5 kgf*cm is 219 to three significant figures, so the value matches its own formula and unit. The finding only works if the unit is misread as N*m; 21.5 N*m is the same quantity in different units (conversion by general unit knowledge: 1 kgf*cm ≈ 0.0981 N*m).
The revision wrote gear_ratio = 2.14, not 21.4, and 2.14 is exactly the chart's 45:21 reduction in row R2.04 (overall 110.2 matches R2.17), so the cited source does hold the written value.

The revision did write control.balance_loop, with plant_mass = 365 g and the same formula as mechanical.assembly.mass ([R11.01] + [R5.07]*[R5.10]; 200 g + 6 × 0.97 oz ≈ 200 + 165 g, using the standard oz-to-g conversion), so the two nodes agree. The firmware note saying only the plant mass changed is accurate; the 'rev 32 unchanged' claim relies on a journal that isn't in the packet and is contradicted by the written node.

The finding's premise is wrong: the revision rewrote firmware.motor_output.pwm_duty_limit to 0.667 (derived from [R1.02] / [R5.04] = 6/9), not left it at 0.833. That gives 0.667 × 9 V ≈ 6 V, which matches the motor's 6 V rating (R1.02), so the motor is not over-driven.

The revision's electrical.imu node sets current_draw to 1.25 mA, the high-performance value (R8.04), not the 0.9 mA normal-mode value. It agrees with electrical.control_board's new 3.3 V × 1.25 mA = 4.13 mW, so the follow-up the finding says is missing is actually there and correct.

The revision wrote electrical.imu.current_draw as value 1.25 with unit "mA", not "mW", which matches R8.04 (1.25 mA, high-performance mode). The control board's derivation of 3.3 V × 1.25 mA ≈ 4.13 mW is consistent with it, so there is no unit error.

The revision rewrites firmware.balance_task with sample_rate 150 Hz, which matches control.balance_loop's 150 Hz and the node's 'equal to the balance-loop period' note. The 100 Hz the reviewer cites is the base value, so the follow-up was a real change and no no_change_justified entry was needed.

The revised control.balance_loop still has torque_peak = 0.145 N*m with source 'derived: [R1.07] * [R1.25]', the same as the base. It was never changed to 0.0726 N*m (that value is the per-motor stall_torque in electrical.motor_left/right), so the justification text is accurate and nothing needs propagating. The arithmetic also checks out: 0.74 kg·cm × 2 = 1.48 kg·cm ≈ 0.145 N*m, using the standard kg·cm to N*m conversion.

The revised control.balance_loop actually writes speed_limit = 51.3 rad/s, not 513. That matches R1.17 exactly: 490 rpm × 2π/60 = 51.3 rad/s, which I checked by ordinary unit-conversion arithmetic. So the conversion or factor-of-ten error the finding describes is not in the design.

Both revised motor nodes record efficiency_point_output_power as 0.8 with unit "W", which matches parts-sheet row R1.20 (0.80 W) from the cited specs page. The "J" unit the finding complains about does not appear in the record, and the derived 2.52 W input and 1.72 W heat values are consistent with it.

The revised electrical.control_board node records sensor_power_draw as 4.13 with unit 'mW', not 'W', and 3.3 V × 1.25 mA = 4.125 mW is correct. The rise from the base 2.97 mW (about 1.16 mW) also matches the regulator's 'about 1.2 mW' justification, so the claimed 1000× unit error is not in the design.

The revision sets the minimum loop rate to 50 Hz, not 5 Hz (a 2x relaxation, not 20x), and the actual balance loop and firmware task stay at 100 Hz, so nothing about the controller as built changes. From general engineering knowledge, not the packet: a robot this size has an unstable pole of a few hertz, so a 50 Hz floor is still about 10x the needed bandwidth, and the base 100 Hz value had no stability analysis behind it either.

The revised mechanical.chassis is not identical to the base: it adds board_lateral_clearance = [R10.08] − [R7.12] = 92 − 69.1 = 22.9 mm, which is a real quantity change answering the new constraint from electrical.control_board. This is the 'fit clearance' that mechanical.assembly's no_change_justified describes, so the record is consistent.

The revised firmware.imu_driver actually sets sample_rate to 416 Hz with a source citing high-performance mode, not the 208 Hz normal-mode text the finding describes. It therefore agrees with the tilt estimator's 416 Hz, the IMU's 1.25 mA (R8.04) and the control board's 4.13 mW (3.3 V x 1.25 mA). From general datasheet knowledge, 416 Hz on the LSM6DS33 does require high-performance mode, so the constrains edge is properly addressed.

The revision writes standby_current_draw as {value: 6, unit: 'uA'}, not 'mA'. That matches parts-sheet row R8.08 (power-down current 6 μA, same LSM6DS33 datasheet URL), so the claimed factor-of-1000 unit error is not there.

The revised mechanical.assembly still gives mass = 330 g, the same as the base, and nowhere in the packet does it read 365 g. By the parts sheet, (200 − 35) g + 6 × 0.97 oz (about 27.5 g each, a unit conversion from general knowledge) ≈ 330 g, so the statement that the plant mass is unchanged is true, and plant_mass = 330 g on control.balance_loop is consistent.

The revised electrical.mcu node records max_supply_voltage as 6.0 V, not 60 V. That matches parts-sheet row R7.09 and the ATmega32U4 datasheet's 6.0 V absolute maximum (general datasheet knowledge), and the derived 1.0 V margin (6.0 − 5) is consistent, so the finding misreads the value.

The revised electrical.battery_pack node gives motor_runtime as 3.14 with unit 'h', not 's'. Redoing the arithmetic gives 7.2 V × 2.2 A·h ÷ (6 V × 0.42 A × 2) = 15.84 W·h ÷ 5.04 W = 3.14 h, so the value and its unit agree and the mismatch the finding describes is not in the revision.

The revision records no_load_current_draw as 0.125 A on both driver nodes, not 125 A. That matches 6 V × 0.150 A / 7.2 V = 0.125 A, so the unit arithmetic balances and the finding misquotes the value.

The revised electrical.battery_cell.energy_capacity has unit 'W*h', not 'J'. 1.2 V × 2200 mAh (2.2 A·h) gives 2.64 W·h, so the units balance and the value is right. The finding describes a unit that the revision did not write.

The revised firmware.imu_driver node records sample_rate = 833 Hz, not 8330 Hz. 833 Hz is on both ODR ladders in R8.09/R8.10 (accelerometer and gyroscope), and it is the lowest rate above 600 Hz, which is twice the 300 Hz task rate, so it matches its own stated source; the electrical nodes were updated to match (1.25 mA high-performance current, 3.3 V × 1.25 mA ≈ 4.13 mW).

In the revised control.balance_loop, plant_mass is still 330 g with the same derivation as the base, so it did not change to 200 g and nothing contradicts the no_change_justified statement. The 330 g figure checks out: 200 g − 35 g + 0.97 oz × 6 (5.82 oz ≈ 165 g) ≈ 330 g. The only change is rate_controller loop_gain going from 2 to 2.5; I used a standard ounce-to-gram conversion.

The revised node sets control.speed_controller loop_gain to 0.3, down from the base value of 0.5. That is a cut, not the sixfold rise to 3 the finding claims. For a plain proportional gain, a smaller value does pass less wheel-speed signal and noise into the tilt set-point (general control knowledge), so the new source text matches the new value.

The revised node actually derives continuous_reaction_moment = 0.0314 N·m from R1.18 × R1.25, not 0.0157 N·m from the URL as the finding says. Either way the value rests on the max-efficiency torque point, which no parts-sheet row presents as a continuous or sustained rating, and no note connects the two (treating max-efficiency torque as continuous duty is only a common engineering proxy). The base chassis node has no such quantity, so the revision introduced the defect.
